cards.title: Model CVR vs. LTV Before Choosing a Subscription Take-Rate Target
cards.summary: Decide subscription take rate and discount depth by modeling contribution margin and retention, not by maximizing subscriber share.
cards.use_when: When setting subscription vs. one-time-purchase defaults, deciding how aggressive your subscribe-and-save discount should be, or reacting to rising CAC.

cards.title: Use Buy-More-Save-More Instead of Flat Percentage Discounts
cards.summary: Bulk/bundle discounts build AOV and attract value-seeking buyers while filtering out pure discount hunters—especially important on low-ticket SKUs.
cards.use_when: When your product is low-ticket (e.g., $20-50) and a flat 10-20% off is not motivating enough to drive subscription take, or when you want to raise AOV without deeper percentage cuts.

cards.title: Stack Value That Doesn't Cost as Much as the Discount It Replaces
cards.summary: Prefer value-stacked offers (products, gifts, bundles) over deeper cash discounts to attract value-seekers rather than discount hunters.
cards.use_when: When designing a subscribe-and-save or acquisition offer and deciding whether to add percentage off, dollar off, a free product, or a bundle.

cards.title: Drive Product Adoption in Onboarding, Not Sales Emails
cards.summary: The first days after purchase should make the customer use and succeed with the product, since retention depends on product experience, not billing mechanics.
cards.use_when: When building the post-purchase onboarding sequence, welcome flow, or first-order unboxing experience for a subscription store.

cards.title: Use Time-Based Check-Ins for Slow-Acting Products
cards.summary: For skincare and supplements that take weeks to show effects, use check-ins and before/after proof to hold subscribers through the payoff period.
cards.use_when: When your product's benefit is delayed (skincare, hormone/menopause supplements, testosterone) and subscribers cancel before they can feel a result.

cards.title: Only Run Gifts in Acquisition or as Targeted Retention Saves
cards.summary: Untargeted post-purchase gifting usually burns margin without incremental retention—either advertise gifts upfront or target them to at-risk/VIP cohorts.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to add a free-gift-on-second-order or a gifting roadmap to a subscription program to reduce churn.

cards.title: Fix the Subscription Portal for Findability First, Not Upsells
cards.summary: Most portal visits are utilitarian (skip, delay, swap, cancel); make the subscription obvious and easy to find before adding sales motion.
cards.use_when: When auditing your subscription customer portal, account login experience, or portal-driven churn.

cards.title: Treat Caveats and Delays as Natural Pre-Churn Signals
cards.summary: Skipping, pausing, and delaying are warning signals—many who delay end up cancelling the upcoming order anyway.
cards.use_when: When monitoring subscriber behavior in the portal or retention dashboard and deciding where to intervene before churn.

cards.title: Know Your Contribution Margin to Choose Between Front-Loaded Profit vs. LTV Tail
cards.summary: Some brands profit on the first order; others accept less upfront for downstream LTV—the choice requires contribution-margin data per order.
cards.use_when: When deciding how much first-order profitability to sacrifice for subscriber LTV, or when setting an aggressive first-order offer.

cards.title: Build a Continuous Offer-Testing Muscle Even as a Small Brand
cards.summary: Start CRO and offer testing early, run multiple funnel hooks, and treat personas, offers, and mechanics as a test matrix rather than a single launch offer.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to invest in offer/CRO testing infrastructure for a store that does not yet have it.

cards.title: Buyer Persona Beats Product Category When Choosing Hooks
cards.summary: Any consumable attracts distinct jobs-to-be-done; hook offers and creative at the buyer's identity or goal, not the product category.
cards.use_when: When writing acquisition ad hooks, offer copy, or landing page angles for a consumable product with multiple use cases.

cards.title: Skip and Delay Controls: Cap Pauses, Make Frequency Adjustment Easy
cards.summary: Replace open-ended pauses with capped skip/delay options, and make cadence changes frictionless because frequency-adjusters retain far longer.
cards.use_when: Designing the subscriber portal for a replenishment/subscription store — deciding which self-serve actions (pause, skip, delay, change frequency) to expose and how to cap them.

cards.title: Push Skippers and Delayers Toward 'Get It Now' or Out the Door
cards.summary: Skipping only defers revenue and may repeat; incentivize immediate orders or let chronic delayers cancel so win-back can work.
cards.use_when: Running a subscriber campaign during a sale or between orders, or when analyzing whether skip/delay behavior is quietly suppressing subscription revenue.

cards.title: Give Subscribers Their Own Offer Track During Sitewide Sales
cards.summary: Never let a sitewide promo undermine your subscriber discount — build a distinct, more valuable subscription offer before planning the sale.
cards.use_when: Planning a sitewide promotion (holiday sale, seasonal event) when a meaningful share of monthly revenue comes from active subscribers.

cards.title: Founder Video Splash Screen on the Cancel Page
cards.summary: A one-minute founder/brand-voice video on the cancel page is the highest-leverage first fix for weak save rates.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding the cancellation flow inside your subscription portal, especially when save rates are low.

cards.title: Six or Seven Cancel Questions, Rotated Monthly, With Cancel Reasons That Change the Copy
cards.summary: Use a small rotating set of cancellation questions and write different reasons-handling copy for each real underlying cause.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the cancellation survey and the save offers attached to each answer in your subscription portal.

cards.title: Turn Cancel Reasons Into a Feedback Loop for Onboarding and Merchandising
cards.summary: Cancellation data is primarily a diagnostic for fixing onboarding, frequency defaults, and value communication — not just a save mechanism.
cards.use_when: Reviewing cancellation survey data after launch, or deciding what to fix in onboarding emails and product pages.

cards.title: Make Cancel Reasons and Redemption Paths Deeply Specific Rather Than Generic
cards.summary: Generic 'don't go!' cancel flows underperform the same depth of specificity applied with a clear founder-voice script and reason-matched offers.
cards.use_when: Writing cancel-flow copy and deciding whether to invest in specific, reason-matched messaging versus a single generic retention screen.

cards.title: Win-Back Offers: Go Broad and Fast Instead of Splitting by Cancel Reason
cards.summary: Rather than one win-back flow per cancellation reason, test aggressive universal win-back offers every week or two for faster, more conclusive results.
cards.use_when: Setting up win-back email/SMS after cancellation, or deciding whether to invest in reason-segmented win-back flows.

cards.title: Dunning and Payment Processing: Expect to Recover 5–10% of Subscription Revenue You're Currently Losing
cards.summary: Most subscription brands lose 5–10% of annual subscription revenue to weak processing and dunning, and the fix is segmented recovery messaging plus better tooling.
cards.use_when: Auditing failed-payment recovery for a store doing millions in annual subscription revenue, or evaluating dunning tools.

cards.title: Treat Subscribers as Their Own Segment With Lower Email Frequency
cards.summary: Active subscribers should be segmented separately from your general list and mailed at lower frequency, with occasional subscriber-specific sends.
cards.use_when: Designing email/SMS campaign calendars for a subscription store where subscribers are a meaningful share of monthly revenue.

cards.title: Extract Maximum Value From Your Subscription Platform CSM and Portal Features
cards.summary: Get your subscription platform's CSM to configure as much as possible inside the portal so your team can focus on email.
cards.use_when: Operating or onboarding a subscription program and deciding how to split work between the platform's native portal and your email/SMS team.

cards.title: Live Your Own Subscription Experience Before Redesigning Offers
cards.summary: Have every team member buy and use the product through the full subscription experience, then compare notes, before testing offers.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing retention and cancellation problems, or before a cancel-flow or offer redesign, when the team is overwhelmed by too many possible changes.

cards.title: Scale ceiling check: AOV × conversion rate > 250
cards.summary: Use the source's AOV-times-conversion-rate benchmark to judge whether an offer has enough headroom to absorb rising ad spend before scaling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase paid traffic spend on an existing offer, or diagnosing why ad scaling stalls even though creatives and targeting look fine.

cards.title: Layer multiple offer types into one structure
cards.summary: Combining a pre-built starter bundle with quantity breaks, tiered free gifts and subscription gating strengthens the offer and raises AOV versus any single mechanic.
cards.use_when: Designing or overhauling the primary offer on a product page to raise average order value and make cold-traffic acquisition viable.

cards.title: Reduce sticker shock with per-serving pricing
cards.summary: Displaying price per serving, bottle or day converts a large bundle price into a small mental unit cost and lowers purchase friction.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a high-AOV bundle or consumable product page where the headline bundle price risks alarming cold traffic.

cards.title: Offer comparison and test one element at a time
cards.summary: Study several proven offer layouts, then test a single change — pricing, quantities, gifts or layout — rather than overhauling everything at once.
cards.use_when: Deciding the scope of an offer redesign on your product page, or planning your first AOV test.

cards.title: Add a scalable starter bundle to lift new-customer AOV
cards.summary: A pre-built starter kit with cheap high-value accessories raises perceived value enough for first-time buyers while letting you charge a little more.
cards.use_when: Designing a first-purchase offer for a consumable or wellness product to raise AOV from cold traffic.

cards.title: Reinforce the offer with delivery, guarantee and reassurance promises
cards.summary: Stacking shipping, stock, delivery-date and guarantee promises near the offer pushes hesitant buyers over the line.
cards.use_when: Adding the final conversion nudges around the buy box on your product page.

cards.title: Structure a listicle advertorial landing page with early CTAs
cards.summary: A '7 reasons why' editorial-style listicle with an author, updated date, image pairs and a CTA placed high up captures cold traffic that never scrolls the whole page.
cards.use_when: Building or revising an advertorial landing page that feeds traffic to your product/offer page.

cards.title: Layer social proof: featured carousel then bulk reviews
cards.summary: Placing a featured review carousel followed by thousands of five-star reviews builds trust before the buyer clicks through to the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding or reordering proof elements on a listicle, product page or checkout to increase purchase trust.

cards.title: Optimise the side cart with 1-click cross-sells and a sticky checkout button
cards.summary: A side cart with easy add-ons, a sticky checkout button and correct savings display raises AOV without adding friction.
cards.use_when: Improving the side cart to lift average order value from shoppers who are already close to buying.

cards.title: Optimise the side cart and sticky checkout for AOV
cards.summary: The side cart is a prime AOV lever: one-click cross-sells, in-cart subscription upgrades and a sticky checkout button capture extra spend with minimal friction.
cards.use_when: Improving the side cart to raise average order value on shoppers already close to buying.

cards.title: Use neuromarketing when surveys contradict sales
cards.summary: Brain-scan research shows consumers cannot accurately report subconscious purchase drivers, so treat stated preferences as unreliable and triangulate with behavioral evidence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to trust customer survey or focus-group feedback when choosing products, positioning, or creative for your store.

cards.title: Avoid the Vampire Effect in ad and PDP imagery
cards.summary: Overtly sexual or extremely beautiful imagery can drain attention from the product being advertised, reducing brand and message recall.
cards.use_when: Selecting hero imagery, lifestyle photography, or influencer creative for ads, PDPs, or landing pages.

cards.title: Turn rituals into repeat-purchase mechanics
cards.summary: Brands gain stickiness by attaching comforting rituals to product use, so build and reinforce a specific consumption ritual around your product.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging, unboxing, onboarding, or retention messaging to increase habitual repeat purchase.

cards.title: Weaponize somatic markers in packaging and page cues
cards.summary: The brain creates emotional 'bookmarks' from past experience, so sensory cues connected to past rewards can trigger purchase without rational deliberation.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging, PDP imagery, sound/video, or unboxing to trigger fast emotional recall tied to prior positive experiences.

cards.title: Use mirror neurons to make product imagery feel firsthand
cards.summary: Seeing someone perform an action fires the same brain regions as doing it, so depict the customer using or enjoying the product to drive desire.
cards.use_when: Choosing product imagery, lifestyle video, or UGC for PDPs, ads, and landing pages.

cards.title: Combine congruent smell and sound with visuals for recall
cards.summary: Buyology finds sight is not the most powerful sense in advertising: congruent smells and sounds paired with visuals exponentially increase brand recall and pleasantness.
cards.use_when: Planning video ads, in-store/retail experience, packaging, or landing page media where multiple senses can be engaged.

cards.title: Design product placement to be integrated, not passive
cards.summary: Buyology's product-placement research found overt, storyline-integrated brand placement is highly memorable while passive, non-integrated placement is forgotten and can even suppress memory.
cards.use_when: Negotiating influencer, content, or media placements and deciding how the brand should appear in the story.

cards.title: Use logo-free brand cues to bypass defensive filters
cards.summary: Buyology demonstrated that logo-free imagery such as a red Ferrari or a sunset can trigger stronger brand cravings than the logos themselves, bypassing conscious defenses.
cards.use_when: Designing ad creative, PDP headers, or brand campaigns when overt logos trigger ad-skipping or skepticism.

cards.title: Do not assume fear-based warnings deter purchase
cards.summary: Buyology found graphic cigarette warnings stimulated the brain's craving spot (nucleus accumbens) rather than deterring smoking, effectively acting as marketing for tobacco.
cards.use_when: Designing warning labels, risk disclosures, or fear-based messaging on PDPs, landing pages, or ads for regulated or high-consideration products.

cards.title: Treat strong brands like belief systems to build loyalty
cards.summary: Buyology found powerful brands activate the same brain regions as religious icons, so building shared belief and ritual around the brand can create devotion-like loyalty.
cards.use_when: Developing brand positioning, community, and retention strategy where the goal is habitual loyalty rather than one-off purchase.

cards.title: Treat traditional market research as one input, not the verdict
cards.summary: Buyology challenges surveys and focus groups because consumers cannot access subconscious motivations, so combine declared research with behavioral and indirect data.
cards.use_when: Planning product-market fit research, pricing tests, or brand positioning studies for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Interview the brain, not the questionnaire: why self-report data misleads ecommerce teams
cards.summary: Conscious answers about why people buy are unreliable because most purchase behaviour runs on autopilot, so ecommerce decisions should be validated with behaviour, not just stated preference.
cards.use_when: Choosing which research inputs to trust when deciding product positioning, PDP copy, or an ad creative direction for an online store.

cards.title: Run a branded versus unbranded test before blaming your product
cards.summary: The Coke-Pepsi fMRI study showed brand associations can override a genuine taste preference, so test your offer both with and without brand cues.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a product page or ad underperforms because of the product/price itself or because the brand story and cues are not doing their job.

cards.title: Build brand equity as emotional value encoding, not just recall
cards.summary: Lindstrom argues emotions are how brains encode value, so brand assets earn their place only when they attach emotional associations to the product.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate budget between brand-building assets (logo, colour, sound, story, packaging) and direct-response tactics for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Diagnose a failing brand like an ambulance crew: five questions
cards.summary: Lindstrom's turnaround routine interrogates the product's distinctive story, forgotten senses and differentiation before any campaign spend.
cards.use_when: A specific SKU or product line is stagnating and you need a structured audit before commissioning new ads or a redesign.

cards.title: Use the three-circle model to combine research methods
cards.summary: Lindstrom places neuromarketing as a third circle alongside quantitative and qualitative research, with the useful insight in the overlap.
cards.use_when: Designing a research plan before a major merchandising, pricing or site redesign decision.

cards.title: Treat disclaimers and negative warnings as potential appetite stimulants
cards.summary: Lindstrom's cigarette-label scans found warnings activated the craving centre rather than suppressing desire, a caution for fear-based ecommerce messaging.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to use scare tactics, negative disclaimers or 'what could go wrong' messaging on a product page, ad or email.

cards.title: Beware the vampire effect: sexual or extreme imagery can eat the brand
cards.summary: Highly sexualised or extremely beautiful imagery can distract viewers so much they fail to remember the brand or product being advertised.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ad creative, PDP imagery or social content that uses attention-grabbing models, shock or extreme beauty.

cards.title: Design for somatic markers: make past reward instantly retrievable
cards.summary: Somatic markers are subconscious bookmarks from past reward or pain that guide purchases without rational deliberation, so stores should make positive past experiences easy to re-trigger.
cards.use_when: Structuring a repeat-purchase flow, homepage, or reorder journey for customers who have bought before.

cards.title: Use mirror neurons to sell the act of using the product
cards.summary: Mirror neurons fire both when someone acts and when they watch the same action, which is why showing a person using a product can trigger the urge to imitate and buy.
cards.use_when: Briefing product photos, video, UGC or influencer content for a PDP or paid social ad.

cards.title: Treat product placement and logo-only branding as weak tools
cards.summary: Lindstrom's study concluded product placement works only in a qualified way and that fragrance and sound are more potent than a logo alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to spend on sponsorships, influencer placements, co-marketing, and logo-heavy creative versus sensory brand assets.

cards.title: Account for short-term reward bias in offers, pricing and BNPL
cards.summary: Princeton scans found immediate rewards triggered stronger emotional activation than larger delayed rewards, meaning instant gratification can beat rational value.
cards.use_when: Designing promotions, discounts, bundle incentives, subscription cadence, or buy-now-pay-later messaging.

cards.title: Design landing pages for the 85 percent autopilot
cards.summary: Since most of the brain is dominated by automatic processes, ecommerce pages should reduce cognitive load and deliver one clear signal rather than requiring deliberation.
cards.use_when: Simplifying a product landing page or PDP where competing elements distract shoppers from the purchase decision.

cards.title: Recognise superstition and ritual as real purchase drivers
cards.summary: Lindstrom argues people act on superstitions and rituals even while denying them, so stores can build belief and repeat-use rituals rather than only rational benefits.
cards.use_when: Building loyalty mechanics, subscription rituals, seasonal moments, or a brand world around a product.

cards.title: Shift budget from collecting data to acting on it
cards.summary: Lindstrom's critique of market research is that companies collect far more data than they can use, so teams should tie every measurement to a specific decision.
cards.use_when: Auditing your analytics stack or planning a research sprint before a merchandising, pricing or creative decision.

cards.title: Use the Wanamaker problem to demand causal tests, not just attribution
cards.summary: The classic admission that half of advertising is wasted without knowing which half remains the core argument for controlled experiments over observational reporting.
cards.use_when: Allocating spend across acquisition channels or deciding which creative, PDP or email variant to keep.

cards.title: Note the high failure rate of new products and test before scaling
cards.summary: Lindstrom cites very high failure rates for new product launches, which argues for cheap validation before committing inventory and media budget.
cards.use_when: Planning a new product launch, new SKU or category expansion for an online store.

cards.title: Use brain-scanning logic to choose what to test on a page
cards.summary: Neuroimaging's practical promise in the source is identifying which marketing efforts are stimulating and memorable versus dull, anxiety-provoking or forgettable.
cards.use_when: Prioritising a CRO backlog when you cannot test everything at once.

cards.title: Pick an ethical line before applying persuasion techniques
cards.summary: Lindstrom frames neuromarketing as a tool like a hammer that can be used well or badly, and says he has turned down projects that crossed his own line.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a dark-pattern, urgency, or fear-based tactic is acceptable for your store, and preparing for customer and regulatory scrutiny.

cards.title: Account for the fact that brands themselves are forgettable by default
cards.summary: Lindstrom argues most brands are the product equivalent of a forgotten hotel room key, filtered out by limited short-term memory unless something makes them worth storing.
cards.use_when: Designing a memorable brand moment across homepage, packaging, unboxing and post-purchase email for an online store.

cards.title: Product placement works only when the brand is part of the narrative
cards.summary: Brand mentions and placements burn into memory only when they play a functional role in the story, not when they run as adjacent ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to integrate a brand into sponsored content, influencer videos, livestreams, unboxing slots or partner media, or judging whether a paid placement is worth the spend.

cards.title: Use mirror neurons to make shoppers mentally rehearse ownership
cards.summary: People's brains simulate actions and experiences they observe, so showing a real person using the product lets customers mentally try it on.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP imagery, video content, UGC, influencer creative or unboxing sequences that should trigger imagined ownership rather than just product specs.

cards.title: Fear-based imagery is memorable — apply it cautiously and ethically
cards.summary: Fear and threat imagery reliably grab attention and memory, as shown in political and ad research, but Lindstrom frames this as a description of what works, not a licence for manipulation.
cards.use_when: Considering problem-agitation angles for a campaign, seasonal promo or retention message where the product solves a genuine risk or pain point.

cards.title: Memory is the ad-effectiveness metric — test recall before and after exposure
cards.summary: Neuromarketing research treats brand recall as the most relevant and reliable proxy for ad effectiveness and a predictor of later purchase.
cards.use_when: Building a measurement plan for a campaign, creative test or sponsorship, especially when clicks and short-term sales don't capture branding effects.

cards.title: Indistinguishable creative destroys brand recall
cards.summary: When competitors imitate each other's visual clichés, viewers cannot tell brands apart and remember none of them.
cards.use_when: Reviewing category ad conventions before producing a campaign, or auditing your own creative for generic category tropes.

cards.title: Design for relevance and fit, not volume of branding
cards.summary: Placements and brand appearances are filtered out when they do not fit the context, so relevance beats sheer frequency.
cards.use_when: Selecting which podcasts, creators, events or media properties to sponsor, or deciding how many brand touches to buy.

cards.title: Use neuro tools to understand emotional attraction, not to read minds
cards.summary: Lindstrom frames neuromarketing as uncovering existing consumer preferences, and combines fast real-time EEG with spatially precise fMRI to get both immediacy and location.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to commission or interpret neuromarketing research for a major brand or product decision, rather than relying on stated preference surveys alone.

cards.title: Integrated product placement suppresses competitor recall
cards.summary: When a brand is deeply woven into content, it not only gets remembered more, it reduces memory for other brands shown around the same content.
cards.use_when: Planning sponsorship exclusivity, retail media buys or co-branded content where you want your brand to dominate the customer's memory in that context.

cards.title: Sequence brand exposure to fire mirror neurons before the price tag
cards.summary: Use observational preference cues (models, aspirational imagery, unboxing) to make shoppers simulate ownership before they evaluate cost.
cards.use_when: Creative strategy and PDP/landing-page design for stores that want to sell aspiration or identity, not just features.

cards.title: Design the dopamine moment: build anticipation into product discovery
cards.summary: Anticipation of reward, not the reward itself, drives the buying impulse — engineer the buildup.
cards.use_when: PDP, collection page, product drop, launch email, or cart design where you want to increase purchase desire.

cards.title: Track your store's daily rituals and attach products to them
cards.summary: BBDO's 26-country research grouped daily behavior into four recurring rituals — embed your product in one.
cards.use_when: Positioning, merchandising, subscription/replenishment design, or content planning when deciding how a product fits into the buyer's day.

cards.title: Build a brand ritual to convert a product feature into a purchase habit
cards.summary: Guinness and Corona turned product quirks into repeatable ceremonies that create emotional attachment and repeat purchase.
cards.use_when: Retail merchandising, unboxing design, café/beverage service steps, or subscription onboarding when you want customers to return out of habit rather than deal-hunting.

cards.title: Redesign unboxing as content owners will film and share
cards.summary: Unboxing is vicarious pleasure — shoppers who watch others open products get much of the same reward as opening them.
cards.use_when: Packaging design, fulfillment inserts, PR/product-drop planning, or UGC acquisition strategy.

cards.title: De-logo your brand: build recognition through owned visual cues
cards.summary: Lindstrom's fMRI work suggests logo-free brand-associated imagery triggered more craving than the logos themselves — design a visual shorthand.
cards.use_when: Brand identity refresh, ad creative, packaging, or store environment design when logo-only assets underperform.

cards.title: Run a logo-free primed campaign once your brand codes are established
cards.summary: Priming works by bypassing the defensive response a visible logo triggers.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative, retargeting ads, or offline media planning where audiences already know the brand and you want to bypass ad-blindness.

cards.title: Subconscious emotion: use faces and scenes to shift willingness to pay
cards.summary: Brief exposure to smiling vs frowning faces changed how much subjects poured and how much they would pay.
cards.use_when: PDP hero imagery, welcome/checkout microcopy, customer-service touchpoints, or pricing experiments.

cards.title: Use mirror neurons to convert the unaffordable into the aspirational future buyer
cards.summary: Watching others use or open products generates vicarious reward even when the viewer cannot buy yet.
cards.use_when: Content planning, creator partnerships, and collection-page merchandising for high-aspiration or high-ticket products.
